audition.title: Our Banking Client — approved Chris voice audition
audition.text:
Here's the challenge in our banking scenario: seventy-five people are testing, but they're sharing just a few environments. So adding AI alone won't remove the bottleneck.

First, make testing repeatable. Give each team an isolated environment and a controlled version of the payment provider. Then bring in GitHub Copilot to help draft tests, and an AI assistant to explain failures in the delivery pipeline.

Now take one test: a payment times out, and the customer retries. Can we prove there's only one debit?

That's the pilot. Better test coverage, faster feedback, and evidence the team can trust. Engineers still review the changes and make the release decision.

slide-1.title: Our Banking Client: shared QA platform
slide-1.text: Let's start with a practical question. How does a banking team improve release confidence when more testers are sharing the same constrained environments? Our Banking Client is a fictional payment scenario with seventy-five offshore quality assurance staff. We will follow the manual work, the platform foundations, and the places where AI can assist. The ambition is repeatable quality at scale. The story describes a proposed path and testable outcomes, not a reported client transformation.

slide-2.title: The QA organization
slide-2.text: The constraint is visible in the team model. Seventy-five people work across five squads, and forty-five focus on manual and domain testing. The opportunity is to make their work easier to repeat, review and reuse, while keeping domain knowledge close to the decisions.

slide-3.title: QE testing scenario: one timeout, two debits
slide-3.text: Here is the payment test scenario. A one-hundred-dollar Canadian transfer is accepted, but the response times out. The customer retries. We deliberately inject a duplicate-posting defect to see whether our tests catch a second debit. The correct result is one transfer, one balanced journal and one customer-visible outcome. This is a testing scenario, not a reported banking incident. It gives the modernization effort a concrete behavior to prove.

slide-4.title: Where the release work goes
slide-4.text: The model follows a bounded release test pack through eight stages. The baseline adds to three hundred hours of hands-on work over a ten-business-day window. That is human effort, not elapsed waiting time. Requirements clarification, data preparation, execution, triage and evidence all contribute. Before buying another tool, identify where people are repeating work and where they are simply blocked. Those two problems require different interventions and different measurements.

slide-5.title: The platform investment
slide-5.text: The platform investment makes useful capabilities available to every squad. Versioned context explains what should happen. Fixtures and controlled dependencies make tests repeatable. Existing frameworks and pipelines run approved changes, and an evidence service preserves the original results. AI helps prepare tests and interpret failures. Application teams still own payment behavior, code review and release decisions. The value comes from connecting these capabilities into the team's existing work.

slide-6.title: Before / after: separate modernization from AI
slide-6.text:
Start with today's manual workflow. People copy cases, prepare shared accounts, wait for a vendor test slot, and reconcile screenshots and logs. Seventy-five testers still face the same environment bottleneck.

Now separate the modernization step. Engineers create reviewed automated tests, isolated data, and validated simulations of the payment provider. The delivery pipeline runs those tests and retains the evidence. That repeatability is valuable even without AI. Real-provider checks still need vendor capacity.

Then add AI assistance. It helps draft cases, test code and fixtures, recommends relevant coverage, and helps explain failures and summarize proof. Engineers review the outputs, existing runners execute, and people make release decisions. Compare equivalent payment packs at all three stages. Measure waiting and reliability separately from AI drafting, review and rework. These are proposed states, not measured client improvements.

slide-11.title: The evidence needed to expand
slide-11.text: Expansion needs evidence that the work is useful and repeatable. Did the test detect an important fault? Did reviewers accept the result without excessive correction? Can another engineer reproduce the run and inspect the original evidence? Compare work of similar scope and retain conventional work as a reference. Faster text generation alone does not answer these questions. The next investment should follow demonstrated quality and net workflow improvement.

slide-17.title: Four layers of AI-assisted QE
slide-17.text: The four layers explain how adoption can grow. Individual copilots help an engineer draft tests and code. Connected workflow assistants use pipeline results to prepare reports. These are capability choices, not four mandatory runtime steps. The platform supports the journey, while each increase in authority needs its own proof.

slide-18.title: Before / after: the shared QE architecture
slide-18.text:
Start on the left. Our Banking Client has seventy-five offshore quality assurance staff, including forty-five manual and domain testers. They share a few test environments. Backend services are not virtualized, and vendor test slots limit parallel runs. Manual execution, reruns and evidence collection add coordination work.

The proposed target is on the right. Squads reuse supported quality engineering services: controlled test data, isolated runs, virtualized dependencies and retained evidence. This foundation lets teams repeat service tests without waiting for every vendor slot.

AI adds assistance with test preparation and interpretation. People still approve expected behavior, review generated changes and make release decisions. Real provider checks remain necessary.

The next slide shows how we will judge this architecture through quality outcomes, alongside effort.

slide-19.title: Outcomes beyond hours
slide-19.text:
Success needs evidence beyond hours saved. We propose three primary measures for the banking pilot.

First, detect every approved critical payment fault that we deliberately introduce. Second, exercise every critical scenario with reviewed assertions and a valid result. Third, make each release decision traceable to its requirements, build, test data and raw results.

Then check the foundation: can the team repeat runs reliably, validate agreed behaviors against the real provider, and help a second squad run independently?

These measures have no recorded baseline or after result yet. We will compare today's workflow, modernized quality engineering, and AI assistance on that foundation. Fewer escaped defects and emergency fixes are business aims to validate across releases. A complete evidence pack can still recommend stopping a release.

slide-20.title: What AI contributes, from requirement to release
slide-20.text:
Let's follow what AI contributes to one banking release. Our example is a payment that times out after acceptance. The customer retries, and the team must prove that the money moves once. First, AI helps clarify the requirement. The product owner confirms the expected behavior.

Second, AI drafts the test scenarios: normal payment, timeout, repeated callback, concurrent retry, and a conflicting request. Domain testers review the coverage and expected outcomes.

Third, AI helps developers write unit tests for retry and duplicate-request logic. These are fast checks of code behavior; they do not replace payment integration tests.

Fourth, AI turns accepted cases into candidate API and user-interface tests. Reviewers require money-movement assertions, not just a successful response.

Fifth, AI helps draft synthetic data and provider simulations. Engineers validate them. Isolated environments and service virtualization make the work repeatable.

Sixth, AI recommends relevant tests or requests an authorized pipeline run. The delivery pipeline executes the tests. Mandatory payment coverage stays in place.

Seventh, AI connects failed assertions with logs and traces, and drafts a diagnosis. The team checks the evidence before accepting the explanation.

Eighth, AI can propose a repair. A developer reviews the change, and the pipeline reruns the tests with fresh data. The expected payment behavior stays fixed.

Ninth, AI assembles a linked release summary and suggests reviewed failures for the regression suite. People decide whether the evidence is sufficient. That is the end-to-end opportunity: less repetitive preparation and investigation, supported by dependable execution and accountable review. This is a proposed workflow to validate in a pilot.

slide-21.title: Follow one payment test through the handoffs
slide-21.text:
Follow the same payment test through six handoffs. The approved requirement says a retry with the same key returns the original transfer and creates no second posting. The reviewed test matrix carries that intent forward.

AI drafts a candidate test. A response-status check alone is too weak, so the reviewer requires the original transfer identifier, one journal, and independently agreed balances. That reviewed test becomes the change we can inspect.

Now challenge the test with a deliberately faulty build. Our illustrative run finds two journals where one was expected. The test fails, and the original failure evidence is retained.

AI links the failed assertion to the journal and trace evidence, and proposes a duplicate-posting diagnosis. An engineer confirms the cause and reviews the proposed fix.

The pipeline performs a fresh retest. The corrected build must pass, while the deliberately faulty variant must still fail. Changing the test simply to accept two debits would invalidate the result.

Finally, the release pack links the requirement, reviewed test, failed run, fix and retest. The release owner checks remaining coverage and real-provider integration evidence. A passing retest is an input to that decision, not automatic approval. All identifiers and results here are authored examples.

slide-4.title: PAY-142: request contract and test oracle
slide-4.text: The request contract defines the oracle. This example transfers ten thousand Canadian cents with a stable idempotency key. Repeating the same key and payload must return the original transfer. Changing the payload under that key must produce a conflict. The expected journal has one transaction and two balanced entries, with the agreed payer and recipient balances. Key scope, retention and recovery rules need explicit agreement with the service owner.

slide-5.title: Timeout and retry: the runtime sequence
slide-5.text: Follow the timeout sequence. The provider accepts the transfer and the journal commits, but the response is lost. The client cannot infer failure from the timeout. It retries with the same key and payload, and the service resolves the original transfer without posting again. The test checks identity, journal count and balances. Run a duplicate-posting variant as well: those same assertions must fail when the defect is present.

Testcontainers can supply disposable dependencies, while WireMock models the provider. Resolve every placeholder to an immutable version, retain preflight results, and keep real-provider integration as a separate check.

Then challenge the same assertions against a correct build and a deliberately defective one. Passing the first and failing the second demonstrates useful fault detection for this scenario.

slide-9.title: The appropriate test layer
slide-9.text: Choose the test layer for the behavior you need to prove. Start with developer unit tests for idempotency-key validation and duplicate-request logic. Copilot can draft JUnit candidates, but developers review the assertions and test doubles. A fake repository cannot establish real payment integration. At the service and API layer, REST Assured and JUnit cover retry, concurrency, conflicts and journal outcomes. At the web layer, Playwright checks the pending state, retry action and final customer message. Keep the owned Selenium and Appium coverage for existing browser and mobile journeys. Batch settlement reconciliation and real-provider sandbox checks remain separate requirements. Generate tests within the appropriate layer; adding a browser framework does not resolve a scarce settlement environment.

slide-31.title: Nine AI-assisted steps, with explicit handoffs
slide-31.text:
Trace one release through nine handoffs. This is AI assistance to an existing payments testing team, distinct from evaluating an AI application. Start with approved context: the payment story, API contract and relevant defects. AI drafts clarification questions. Product and domain QA approve the rule that a same-key, same-payload retry returns the original transfer without a second posting.

Next, test design produces a reviewed matrix. AI proposes timeout, duplicate callback, concurrency and conflicting-payload cases. Domain QA supplies the expected behavior independently of the implementation. A written case is an input to executable test code, not the code itself.

The developer unit-test step uses the handler source and accepted behavior. Copilot can draft JUnit candidates for key validation and duplicate-request logic. The developer checks the fake repository and verifies one insertion for repeated calls. A passing unit test does not establish correctness across the real database and provider.

The API and user-interface step turns the reviewed matrix into a pull request. REST Assured tests exercise the payment service; selected Playwright checks cover the customer's pending state and retry action. Reviewers require the original transfer identifier, one journal, and balances of ninety thousand and ten thousand minor units. A status-only assertion is rejected.

Data and provider behavior are versioned inputs. AI can draft synthetic seed scripts and WireMock mappings for acceptance followed by a timeout. Engineers validate those mappings against the provider contract. Testcontainers and the delivery pipeline supply repeatable resources. Real-provider and settlement checks remain separate requirements.

For execution, AI may recommend affected tests or request an authorized pipeline job. Azure Pipelines runs the approved suite and publishes raw JUnit results and traces. The mandatory payment suite cannot be silently omitted. Record the build, test commit, fixture and stub versions under the run identifier.

During investigation, AI reads retained evidence and proposes a cause. In our injected-defect example, the assertion expects one journal but observes two. The defect draft must link that evidence. A reviewer confirms the diagnosis, and the original failing verdict remains unchanged.

For repair, AI may propose a source change for developer review. Keep the accepted payment assertions fixed. The pipeline uses a fresh run identifier and isolated data for the retest. The corrected build must pass, and the deliberate duplicate-posting variant must still fail.

For release evidence, AI drafts a summary of coverage, run results, reviewed dispositions and missing checks. The release owner reviews the linked pack, including required real-provider evidence. Accepted defects can become reviewed regression cases. The shared platform provides context access, artifact versions, scoped pipeline access and evidence retention across these steps; it does not replace the named owners.

slide-26.title: What AI contributes, from requirement to release
slide-26.text:
Let's follow what AI contributes to one banking release. Our example is a payment that times out after acceptance. The customer retries, and the team must prove that the money moves once. First, AI helps clarify the requirement. The product owner confirms the expected behavior.

Second, AI drafts the test scenarios: normal payment, timeout, repeated callback, concurrent retry, and a conflicting request. Domain testers review the coverage and expected outcomes.

Third, AI helps developers write unit tests for retry and duplicate-request logic. These are fast checks of code behavior; they do not replace payment integration tests.

Fourth, AI turns accepted cases into candidate API and user-interface tests. Reviewers require money-movement assertions, not just a successful response.

Fifth, AI helps draft synthetic data and provider simulations. Engineers validate them. Isolated environments and service virtualization make the work repeatable.

Sixth, AI recommends relevant tests or requests an authorized pipeline run. The delivery pipeline executes the tests. Mandatory payment coverage stays in place.

Seventh, AI connects failed assertions with logs and traces, and drafts a diagnosis. The team checks the evidence before accepting the explanation.

Eighth, AI can propose a repair. A developer reviews the change, and the pipeline reruns the tests with fresh data. The expected payment behavior stays fixed.

Ninth, AI assembles a linked release summary and suggests reviewed failures for the regression suite. People decide whether the evidence is sufficient. That is the end-to-end opportunity: less repetitive preparation and investigation, supported by dependable execution and accountable review. This is a proposed workflow to validate in a pilot.

slide-2.title: The enterprise assurance platform
slide-2.text:
Let's walk through the whole architecture. These boxes are responsibilities; they do not require eleven new products. Follow one banking test from a request to reviewed evidence. This is a proposed design and an authored testing scenario, not a report of a live client implementation.

Start with the engineer. A payment provider accepts a transfer, but the customer sees a timeout and retries. The test must prove that the retry creates one transfer and one balanced journal, not two debits. The product owner and domain tester approve that expected behavior before AI drafts anything.

Delivery systems supply the source material: the payment story, API contract, repository revision and previous defects. Azure Boards or Jira can hold the story; GitHub or Azure DevOps can hold the code and pipeline. The important output is a traceable set of versions, not a particular vendor.

The context service selects the material this task is allowed to use. It removes unnecessary data and records an input snapshot. For our retry test, that includes the idempotency rule, provider behavior and relevant test helpers. Missing or contradictory requirements go back to a person for clarification.

The quality engineering runtime turns that context into a plan and a proposed test change. It records the model and prompt versions, with limits on retries and resource use. A coding assistant can draft a JUnit test with REST Assured. That draft still needs review; it cannot redefine the payment rule.

Next, the action gateway checks the requested operation, target environment and approval. It can permit a test run in the approved sandbox. A request outside that scope is stopped or escalated, with a recorded reason. Permission comes from this control, not from the model saying that an action is safe.

The sandbox runs the real payment service and database against controlled fixtures. Testcontainers can provide isolated resources; WireMock can reproduce the provider accepting a payment before returning a timeout. The test retries with the same key and checks transfers, journal entries and balances. A deliberately introduced duplicate-debit fault should make the test fail. A green build alone is insufficient.

Now look at AI applications at the top right. This is a second entry into assurance. If the bank changes an AI assistant or agent, its versioned application configuration enters evaluation. It is not a required extra step inside every payment API call.

The evaluation service compares candidate behavior with independent expected results on held-out cases. Held-out means those cases were reserved for assessment, rather than used to tune the candidate. Human reviewers label important examples and calibrate any model-based judges. For an AI failure-summary assistant, check whether its explanation matches the raw test evidence. It must not turn a failed assertion into a pass.

Sandbox checks and applicable AI evaluations send their evidence to the release authority. The accountable reviewer uses existing pipeline and change gates to approve, hold or roll back. Missing evidence or a failed critical payment assertion means hold. The agent that generated the change cannot approve itself.

The evidence store retains run identifiers, input versions, proposed artifacts, raw results and the release decision. The dashed arrows represent these context and evidence relationships, not another execution sequence. For the retry scenario, a reviewer should be able to trace the one-transfer assertion back to its rule and reproduce the run.

Finally, people curate useful failures into the regression corpus. Each accepted case has a reviewed expectation and a version. The feedback path challenges later AI application versions. Keep assessment cases separate from tuning examples, and maintain payment regression tests in the normal test repository. Learning is reviewed curation, not automatic acceptance of model output.

This depends on repeatable environments, controlled test data, service virtualization, reliable pipelines and named owners. Where vendor test slots are scarce, controlled substitutes expand repeatable testing; separate checks against the real provider remain necessary. The outcome to demonstrate is a repeatable payment test, an independently detected fault and a traceable decision. AI assists the work. Modernized testing makes it dependable.

slide-10.text: Mutation-guided generation starts from a fault concern. Select a meaningful change, generate a candidate test, and preserve the intended assertion. The candidate must pass the original implementation and fail the faulty variant for the intended reason. Exclude invalid or equivalent mutations before judging the result. Retain the fault rationale with the run evidence. Detecting selected mutations improves the challenge but does not prove that every real defect is covered.

slide-12.text: Flaky-test repair must preserve test meaning. Reproduce the unstable behavior and collect its conditions before proposing a change. Deleting a check may make a test stable while hiding the original problem. Retain repeatability evidence and reject repairs that trade away fault detection.

slide-13.title: The evaluation corpus lifecycle
slide-13.text: The evaluation corpus has its own lifecycle. Curate permitted examples and reviewed failures, remove near duplicates, and label expected behavior. Version the source, expectation, scenario tag and review decision. Report important slices rather than relying only on an overall result.

Critical disagreements may require a deterministic check or expert gate instead of a larger average score.

slide-15.title: The tool authority boundary
slide-15.text: This exercise tests the boundary between untrusted content and tool authority. Test recovery as well as the model's verbal refusal.

slide-18.text: Release decisions begin with comparable runs and mandatory floors. Use the same held-out corpus and versioned conditions to examine behavior, regression, denial and workflow limits. A failed critical scenario triggers a hold and investigation even if the average improves. When floors hold, reviewers inspect remaining regressions and uncertainty before a bounded rollout. Agree the thresholds locally and retain the scenario-level decision evidence.

slide-19.title: Containment, fallback and recovery
slide-19.text: Recovery protects the underlying business process. A severe regression, outage or policy event can trigger containment and stop consequential actions. Reverting a model does not undo an external side effect. Compensation and reconciliation therefore need their own tested runbooks.

slide-20.text: Operational evidence joins application events, gateway decisions and reviewer feedback by run identifier. Operations uses failures and tail latency; platform owners inspect tool patterns and denials; evaluation owners curate reviewed cases. This shared evidence makes incidents actionable and feeds future checks. A monitoring dashboard without reliable joins cannot explain how a particular result was produced.

Reviews capture acceptance, correction and human effort. Outcomes connect those artifacts to rework and quality over a defined period. Compare matched cohorts and include preparation, verification and unsuccessful attempts. Time saved requires a separate mechanism before it becomes realized value.

Reviewers add the sanitized failure case to regression and verify recovery. This illustrates a test to implement, not proof that all possible paths are covered.

Enforce tool authority externally because actions can have consequences beyond the response. Retain the versions, assertions and decisions that let another engineer inspect whether these design choices actually hold.

slide-28.title: Failure semantics are part of the contract

These behaviors keep an unavailable dependency from becoming an unexplained success.

slide-33.title: Containerization, virtualization and contracts

slide-35.title: Measuring the incremental AI effect

First separate modernization improvements from the additional effect of AI. The decision to expand should follow accepted outcomes and complete effort, with uncertainty visible.

slide-36.title: Nine AI-assisted steps, with explicit handoffs
slide-36.text:
Trace one release through nine handoffs. This is AI assistance to an existing payments testing team, distinct from evaluating an AI application. Start with approved context: the payment story, API contract and relevant defects. AI drafts clarification questions. Product and domain QA approve the rule that a same-key, same-payload retry returns the original transfer without a second posting.

Next, test design produces a reviewed matrix. AI proposes timeout, duplicate callback, concurrency and conflicting-payload cases. Domain QA supplies the expected behavior independently of the implementation. A written case is an input to executable test code, not the code itself.

The developer unit-test step uses the handler source and accepted behavior. Copilot can draft JUnit candidates for key validation and duplicate-request logic. The developer checks the fake repository and verifies one insertion for repeated calls. A passing unit test does not establish correctness across the real database and provider.

The API and user-interface step turns the reviewed matrix into a pull request. REST Assured tests exercise the payment service; selected Playwright checks cover the customer's pending state and retry action. Reviewers require the original transfer identifier, one journal, and balances of ninety thousand and ten thousand minor units. A status-only assertion is rejected.

Data and provider behavior are versioned inputs. AI can draft synthetic seed scripts and WireMock mappings for acceptance followed by a timeout. Engineers validate those mappings against the provider contract. Testcontainers and the delivery pipeline supply repeatable resources. Real-provider and settlement checks remain separate requirements.

For execution, AI may recommend affected tests or request an authorized pipeline job. Azure Pipelines runs the approved suite and publishes raw JUnit results and traces. The mandatory payment suite cannot be silently omitted. Record the build, test commit, fixture and stub versions under the run identifier.

During investigation, AI reads retained evidence and proposes a cause. In our injected-defect example, the assertion expects one journal but observes two. The defect draft must link that evidence. A reviewer confirms the diagnosis, and the original failing verdict remains unchanged.

For repair, AI may propose a source change for developer review. Keep the accepted payment assertions fixed. The pipeline uses a fresh run identifier and isolated data for the retest. The corrected build must pass, and the deliberate duplicate-posting variant must still fail.

For release evidence, AI drafts a summary of coverage, run results, reviewed dispositions and missing checks. The release owner reviews the linked pack, including required real-provider evidence. Accepted defects can become reviewed regression cases. The shared platform provides context access, artifact versions, scoped pipeline access and evidence retention across these steps; it does not replace the named owners.
